blocks.text:
Ask any large engineering organization what sits underneath their session store, their shopping cart, or their user-preferences service, and there is a decent chance the answer is a distributed key-value store: something built in the spirit of Amazon's Dynamo or Apache Cassandra. It has a deceptively small API, usually just get and put keyed by a single identifier, but underneath that simplicity is one of the richest problems in all of distributed systems: how do you keep data available and fast across a fleet of machines, any of which can fail at any moment, without ever losing a write or serving obviously wrong data?

This is not a question about clever query languages or complex joins. There are no joins here at all. It is a question about partitioning (which machine owns which piece of the keyspace), replication (how many copies of each piece of data exist, and where), and failure handling (what happens the instant one of those machines goes quiet). Get those three things right and the rest of the system nearly falls into place.

We are going to design a distributed, horizontally-scalable key-value store that supports simple get and put operations, tolerates individual node failures without losing data, and lets the operator tune how strongly consistent versus how available the system behaves, because as we will see, you genuinely cannot have maximum amounts of both at the same time.

["Put: store a value under a given key, replicated across multiple nodes for durability.","Get: retrieve the value stored under a given key.","Delete: remove a key and its value.","Automatic partitioning: keys are automatically distributed across all nodes in the cluster without manual sharding by the client.","Elastic membership: nodes can join or leave the cluster, and the system rebalances data without a full outage."]
items: Put: store a value under a given key, replicated across multiple nodes for durability.
Get: retrieve the value stored under a given key.
Delete: remove a key and its value.
Automatic partitioning: keys are automatically distributed across all nodes in the cluster without manual sharding by the client.
Elastic membership: nodes can join or leave the cluster, and the system rebalances data without a full outage.

blocks.text: Notice how short this list is. That brevity is the whole point of a key-value store: the API surface is intentionally tiny so that the underlying engine can focus entirely on being fast, available, and resilient, rather than on expressive query capability.

["High availability: the cluster should keep serving both reads and writes even while some nodes are down.","Horizontal scalability: adding nodes should linearly increase capacity and throughput, without a central bottleneck.","Tunable consistency: different applications built on top of this store have different needs, so consistency strength should be a per-operation dial, not a fixed global setting.","Low latency: single-digit-millisecond reads and writes for the common case.","Durability: an acknowledged write should not be lost, even if the node that first received it crashes moments later."]
items: High availability: the cluster should keep serving both reads and writes even while some nodes are down.
Horizontal scalability: adding nodes should linearly increase capacity and throughput, without a central bottleneck.
Tunable consistency: different applications built on top of this store have different needs, so consistency strength should be a per-operation dial, not a fixed global setting.
Low latency: single-digit-millisecond reads and writes for the common case.
Durability: an acknowledged write should not be lost, even if the node that first received it crashes moments later.

blocks.text: Consider a cluster backing a mid-size application with 50 million keys and a combined read-plus-write rate of 100,000 operations per second at peak, split roughly 70 percent reads and 30 percent writes. That works out to about 70,000 reads per second and 30,000 writes per second. Spread across a cluster of, say, 20 nodes, each node needs to sustain roughly 100,000 divided by 20, which is 5,000 operations per second, well within reach of a single well-tuned node handling in-memory-plus-SSTable storage.

blocks.text: If the average key-value pair is 1KB, 50 million keys is 50GB of logical data. With a replication factor of 3, the actual physical storage requirement triples to 150GB total across the cluster, or about 150GB divided by 20 nodes, which is 7.5GB per node, comfortably fitting on a single machine's disk with plenty of headroom for growth.

blocks.text: Every request, whether a get or a put, starts at a coordinator, which in this design is not a special, separate machine but simply whichever storage node the client happens to talk to first (any node can act as coordinator for any key, which is important for avoiding a single point of failure). The coordinator hashes the key to figure out which nodes on the ring own that key's data, forwards the request to the appropriate replicas, and waits for enough of them to respond before answering the client.

["put(key, value, consistencyLevel) writes a value under a key, waiting for the requested write quorum before returning.","get(key, consistencyLevel) reads the value under a key, waiting for the requested read quorum and resolving any version conflicts among the replicas that responded.","delete(key) removes a key, implemented internally as a special tombstone write rather than an immediate physical delete, so the deletion itself can replicate correctly."]
items: put(key, value, consistencyLevel) writes a value under a key, waiting for the requested write quorum before returning.
get(key, consistencyLevel) reads the value under a key, waiting for the requested read quorum and resolving any version conflicts among the replicas that responded.
delete(key) removes a key, implemented internally as a special tombstone write rather than an immediate physical delete, so the deletion itself can replicate correctly.

blocks.title: Why deletes are tombstones, not immediate removals
blocks.text: If a node deletes a key locally and immediately forgets it ever existed, a later anti-entropy repair comparing it against a replica that still has the old value could mistake that old value for "missing data" and resurrect it. Writing a tombstone, a special marker meaning "this key was deleted at time T", and only physically removing it after enough time has passed for the deletion to have replicated everywhere, avoids that resurrection bug entirely.

Writing a tombstone, a special marker meaning "this key was deleted at time T", and only physically removing it after enough time has passed for the deletion to have replicated everywhere, avoids that resurrection bug entirely.

blocks.text: Internally, each storage node organizes its data the way most modern key-value engines do: an in-memory memtable absorbs writes first, since writing to memory is essentially free, and periodically flushes to an immutable, sorted SSTable on disk once it fills up. A background compaction process periodically merges older SSTables together, discarding overwritten and tombstoned data along the way.

An entity relationship style diagram showing a keyspace divided into partitions, each partition replicated onto multiple nodes with a defined role

blocks.text: The single most important structural decision in this entire system is how data gets spread across nodes, and the answer is consistent hashing. Imagine mapping every node, and every key, onto points on a circle using a hash function. A key belongs to whichever node is the first one encountered walking clockwise from the key's position. The elegant part is what happens when a node joins or leaves: only the keys between the new node and its immediate neighbor need to move, not the entire keyspace, which is a dramatic improvement over naive modulo-based hashing, where adding a single node would reshuffle almost everything.

blocks.text: In practice, each physical node is represented by many virtual nodes scattered around the ring rather than a single point, which smooths out load distribution (without virtual nodes, an unlucky hash placement could leave one physical node responsible for a much larger arc of the ring than its peers) and makes rebalancing after a node join or leave spread evenly across many existing nodes instead of dumping all the migrated load onto one unlucky neighbor.

blocks.alt: A worked-example sequence diagram: a coordinator writes to node 1 and node 3 successfully, but node 2 is temporarily down, so node 1 stores a hint on node 2's behalf, and delivers it once node 2 recovers

blocks.text: Picture a write with N equals 3 landing while Node 2 is momentarily unreachable, perhaps mid-restart after a routine deploy. The coordinator successfully writes to Node 1 and Node 3, easily satisfying a write quorum of W equals 2, and returns success to the client immediately, since two out of three replicas is enough. Rather than simply giving up on Node 2 entirely, Node 1 stores a small hint, essentially a note saying "this write belongs to Node 2, please deliver it once it is back." A few minutes later, when Node 2 rejoins the cluster and its gossip heartbeat is seen again, Node 1 delivers the queued hint, and Node 2 catches up to full consistency without ever needing an expensive full repair.

blocks.text: If Node 2 stays down long enough that the hint itself expires before delivery, that is exactly what the background anti-entropy repair process (using Merkle trees, discussed in section 20) is there to catch, comparing replicas at a coarser granularity and reconciling anything that hinted handoff missed.

blocks.text: The memtable itself already functions as a natural, always-warm cache for the most recently written data, since any read for a key still sitting in the memtable is served straight from memory without touching disk at all. Beyond that, application teams building on top of this store are encouraged to add their own read-through cache layer in front of it for extremely hot, read-heavy keys, the same way one might in front of a traditional database, since a distributed key-value store optimized for durability and availability is not automatically the fastest possible read path for a single wildly popular key.

blocks.text: Gossip itself is a lightweight, continuous, asynchronous background process, not something any client request waits on. Anti-entropy repair likewise runs as a scheduled background job per node, comparing Merkle tree hashes of its data against a peer's and only transferring the specific key ranges that actually differ, rather than a full, expensive data dump between every pair of replicas.

blocks.text: Because any node can coordinate any request, load balancing largely happens for free: a smart client driver can maintain its own view of the ring and either talk directly to a replica that actually owns the key (skipping an extra network hop entirely) or round-robin across the cluster if it prefers simplicity over that optimization.

blocks.text: Scaling this system is, almost by design, just a matter of adding more nodes to the ring. Consistent hashing ensures that adding one new node only requires migrating roughly 1 divided by (number of nodes) of the total data, a small, bounded amount of rebalancing rather than a disruptive full reshuffle.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing an N equals 3, W equals 2, R equals 2 configuration satisfying the W plus R greater than N rule, guaranteeing strongly consistent reads

blocks.text: Replication in this system is governed by three numbers: N, how many replicas of each piece of data exist; W, how many replicas must acknowledge a write before it is considered successful; and R, how many replicas must respond to a read before it is returned to the client. With N equals 3, W equals 2, and R equals 2, the classic rule W plus R greater than N holds (2 plus 2 equals 4, which is greater than 3), which mathematically guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum share at least one overlapping replica, meaning a read is guaranteed to see the most recent successful write. Tune W and R lower (say W equals 1, R equals 1) and you get lower latency and higher availability at the cost of that overlap guarantee, which is the tunable consistency knob mentioned back in the non-functional requirements.

A CAP theorem diagram showing this system choosing availability with partition tolerance, achieving tunable consistency rather than strict consistency

blocks.text: This is the textbook CAP theorem teaching example. Partition tolerance is not optional, a network will partition eventually no matter how good the infrastructure is, so the real choice is between consistency and availability during that partition. This design defaults to AP (available, partition tolerant) with tunable consistency layered on top through the W and R quorum knobs from the previous section, rather than forcing a single global CP or AP choice. An application that genuinely needs strong consistency can set W and R high enough to guarantee overlap; an application that prizes low latency above all else can set them low and accept a small, well-understood risk of reading slightly stale data.

blocks.text: Hinted handoff (section 13) handles brief outages gracefully. Longer outages or genuinely lost hints are caught by anti-entropy repair, which uses a Merkle tree, a hash tree where each parent node's hash is derived from its children's hashes, to compare two replicas efficiently: if two replicas' root hashes match, their data is identical and no further comparison is needed at all; if they differ, the mismatch can be narrowed down to the specific subtree, and eventually the specific key range, that actually differs, without ever needing to compare every single key directly.

blocks.text: Client-to-node and node-to-node traffic should run over TLS, since gossip and replication traffic carries the actual data being stored. Authentication should be enforced at the client-driver level with per-keyspace credentials, and authorization should scope which keyspaces a given credential can read from or write to, since a multi-tenant deployment of this store might host unrelated teams' data on the same physical cluster.

blocks.text: The metrics that matter most here are per-node latency percentiles (a single slow node drags down every quorum operation that touches it), hinted handoff queue depth (a growing queue signals a node has been down longer than expected), gossip convergence time (how quickly the cluster agrees on membership changes), and repair lag (how far behind the anti-entropy process has fallen). A sudden divergence between two replicas' data, caught by monitoring the repair process's findings, is often the earliest signal that something is subtly wrong somewhere in the write path.

blocks.alt: A map of two bottlenecks: a coordinator overwhelmed by fan-out writes, fixed by letting any node coordinate to spread the load, and a few extremely hot keys, fixed by client-side caching in front of the store

blocks.text: Because any node can coordinate, there is no single fixed gateway to become a bottleneck the way there would be in a system with dedicated coordinator machines. The more realistic pressure point is a small number of extremely hot keys landing on the same handful of physical nodes, since consistent hashing guarantees even distribution of the keyspace but says nothing about even distribution of access frequency.

blocks.alt: A comparison of last-write-wins conflict resolution using timestamps versus vector clocks tracking causal history

blocks.text: When two writes to the same key happen concurrently on different replicas (both unaware of each other, which is entirely possible in a distributed system with no single writer lock), something has to decide which one wins. Last-write-wins, simply comparing timestamps and keeping the newer one, is simple to implement and reason about, but it can silently discard a legitimate concurrent write if clocks are even slightly skewed. Vector clocks track the causal history of a value across replicas precisely enough to detect true concurrency (as opposed to one write happening-before another), but push the actual conflict-resolution decision up to the application, which now has to know how to merge two conflicting versions of its own data.

blocks.text: The choice of gossip over a centralized membership service is itself a trade-off: gossip has no single point of failure and scales gracefully as the cluster grows, at the cost of membership changes taking a small, bounded amount of time to fully propagate, rather than being instantly consistent everywhere the moment they happen.

blocks.alt: A cost breakdown dominated by disk storage multiplied by the replication factor, plus compute for the coordinator and node processes

blocks.text: Replication is the dominant cost driver, since a replication factor of 3 means paying for three times the raw storage of the logical data. Tiering older, cold key ranges onto cheaper storage classes, and compacting SSTables aggressively to reclaim space from tombstoned and overwritten data, are the two most effective levers for controlling that cost without touching the replication factor itself, which exists for durability reasons that should not be compromised lightly.

import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from typing import List, Protocol


class StorageNode(Protocol):
    def write(self, key: str, value: str) -> bool: ...


# Coordinates a write across N replicas, succeeding once W of them
# acknowledge, without waiting for the remaining, slower replicas.
class QuorumCoordinator:
    def __init__(self, write_quorum: int):
        self._write_quorum = write_quorum

    def write_with_quorum(self, replicas: List[StorageNode], key: str, value: str) -> bool:
        acked = threading.Event()
        count = 0
        lock = threading.Lock()

        def do_write(replica: StorageNode) -> None:
            nonlocal count
            ok = replica.write(key, value)
            if ok:
                with lock:
                    count += 1
                    if count >= self._write_quorum:
                        acked.set()

        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(replicas)) as pool:
            for replica in replicas:
                pool.submit(do_write, replica)
            met_quorum = acked.wait(timeout=0.5)
        return met_quorum
